tour.title: Varanasi: Life, Death and the Ganges
tour.summary: Dawn bells at Assi, poets and kings along the river stairs, lunch in the old-city lanes, and the evening lamps of Dashashwamedh — one walk through the oldest living city on earth.
tour.overviewText:
Welcome to Varanasi. Or Banaras. Or Kashi, the Luminous — the city of light, which is what the oldest texts call it. Nobody has managed to prove it isn't the oldest living city on earth, and three thousand years of continuous living, praying and cremating on this riverbank make a strong case.

Start with the death, because everything else here orbits it. Most Hindus believe life runs in a cycle — birth, death, rebirth, repeat — and the great prize is getting off the wheel for good. That exit has a name, moksha, liberation, and Varanasi is where it is on offer: to die here, to be cremated on these ghats with your ashes scattered in this river, is to step out of the cycle entirely. So this is where India comes to die. Sons carry their fathers on bamboo biers off trains. Families travel for days with their dead. Old people move into hospices like Mumukshu Bhavan and Kashi Labh Mukti Bhavan for the express purpose of dying within city limits. The wood smoke over the water is not scenery. It is the reason the city exists.

The walk itself is simple. We start at dawn at Assi Ghat in the south and follow the river north: saints, kings, cremations, one very southern god. Mid-morning we turn inland for the golden temple and the lanes that feed pilgrims by the thousand. Then back to the river at Manikarnika — viewed from the path, quietly — and we end at the quiet northern ghats, where a temple is slowly tipping into the Ganges.

Modern Varanasi wears its holiness in public. This is the prime minister's constituency — Narendra Modi has held this seat since 2014 — and the Kashi Vishwanath Corridor, opened in 2021, bulldozed a dense old neighbourhood to give pilgrims a grand walkway to the temple. Supporters call it overdue renewal; critics mourn what was demolished to build it. You will walk the result. And the Ganges itself is both goddess and open sewer: the Namami Gange cleanup has made stretches visibly better, and plenty of stretches are not. Hold the sacred and the polluted in your head at the same time. So does everyone here.

Two house rules before we start. Rule one: the ghats are steps — hundreds of them, steep, uneven, and slippery near the water. This walk is not step-free, and I will not pretend otherwise. Wear shoes with grip, not flip-flops, and budget your knees. Rule two: every price I mention is an educated guess. Indian prices move, temple rules change, and the aarti starts when it starts. Verify at the gate, check the day's timings, and never blame the nice voice in your ear.

And one last thing, and this one matters. Varanasi is not a museum. People bathe, mourn, marry, eat and argue all around you, often at the same time. Walk slowly. Do not photograph bathers or cremations. When I tell you to put the camera away, I mean it. The river rewards the patient and embarrasses the hurried.
tour.difficulty: Moderate. Mostly flat walking along the ghat tops, but with many steep, uneven stone steps up and down between ghats and the old-city lanes. Ghat steps are not step-free and can be slippery near the water.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start at dawn, around 5:30 to 6am at Assi, for the morning aarti, soft light and the ghats at their most alive. Time the middle of the walk for the temple and lunch, and be back at the river for the Dashashwamedh evening aarti at about 7pm — either linger along the way or rest midday and return. Winter mornings can be foggy, which is atmospheric but slow.

stops.name: Assi Ghat
stops.narration:
Good morning — and I mean that precisely, because at Assi Ghat the morning is the whole point. This is the southern end of the great staircase riverfront, and before the heat and the crowds arrive, the city does its most serious business here: bells, chanting, yoga on the steps, and the Subah-e-Banaras program — a staged dawn of prayer and classical music that the city puts on every sunrise.

The name is older than all of that. They say the goddess Durga flung her sword down here after killing two demons, and the sword — assi — gouged out the little stream that once met the Ganges at this spot. The stream is mostly gone. The story stuck around, which tells you how this city files things.

Two things to absorb while the light is good. First, the ghats are infrastructure, not scenery: laundry, buffalo baths, wrestling pits — the akharas up the lanes, traditional wrestling gyms where athletes train at ungodly hours — all of it runs on these steps. Second, dawn is a strategy, not just poetry. By ten the stone is an oven and the riverfront belongs to the touts. You got here first. Enjoy the brief period today when Varanasi is showing off only for you.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open ghat, no ticket and no gate. Boatmen will offer sunrise rides from about ₹100 to ₹300 per person for a shared boat; agree the price and duration before stepping in.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. The Subah-e-Banaras morning ceremony runs around sunrise, roughly 5:30 to 7am depending on season. Timings shift with the sun, so check locally.
stops.accessibility: Broad steps down to the water with no ramps and no handrails. The upper promenade is level but the steps themselves are steep and uneven.
stops.insiderTip: Come before sunrise and claim a spot on the middle steps. The morning aarti faces east across the water, and the first light hits the priests' lamps before it hits anything else.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north along the top of the ghats, keeping the river on your right, for about five minutes. The next stop is the quieter ghat with the large peepal tree and the small shrines, just past the bend.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Vijendra319, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Tulsi Ghat
stops.narration:
One man sat above this river and wrote the book that hundreds of millions of Hindus grow up hearing.

Tulsidas lived here in the 1500s — his house is said to have stood right above these steps — and did something radical: he retold the Ramayana, the ancient epic of Prince Rama, in Awadhi, the language ordinary people actually spoke. Until then the great stories belonged to priests who read Sanskrit, a language of scholarship most people never learned. Tulsidas took the gods out of the library and handed them to the street. Hinduism's biggest bestseller was a translation.

Behind the ghat sits Lolark Kund, a stepped well sacred to Surya, the sun, worshipped here as a god — childless couples still come to bathe and pray for a child. Nobody can prove it works. Everybody comes anyway, which tells you how this city weighs evidence.

And look for the modern footnote: the Sankat Mochan Foundation, run for decades by Veer Bhadra Mishra, a temple priest who also happened to be a hydraulics professor, campaigning to clean the Ganga. Faith and sewage treatment, same office. Only in Varanasi does the holiest man in the neighbourhood also read water-quality reports.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open ghat, no ticket. The Lolark Kund well behind the ghat is also free to visit.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. The ghat is at its best and busiest around sunrise and sunset.
stops.accessibility: Steep stone steps with no ramps. The lanes behind the ghat are narrow and uneven.
stops.insiderTip: Glance at the painted tiles and wall shrines as you pass — the Ramlila scenes painted around these lanes are touched up every autumn before the festival season.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue north along the ghat-top path for about ten to twelve minutes, passing Bhadaini and Janaki ghats. The next stop is the ghat with the tall crematorium building and the big open burning terraces on your right.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Nandanupadhyay, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Harishchandra Ghat
stops.narration:
Lower your voice. This is Harishchandra Ghat, the smaller of the city's two burning ghats, and what happens here is not for you — it just happens in front of you.

The name is a whole moral education. King Harishchandra, legend says, gave up his kingdom, his wife and nearly his son rather than tell a lie, and ended up destitute, working this cremation ground for the Dom keeper of the pyres — hauling corpses, gathering firewood. The Doms are the hereditary cremation keepers of Varanasi, the community that has run these fires for generations: among the most essential and least honoured jobs in the city. The gods restored Harishchandra in the end. His name is still the local shorthand for a person who will not bend the truth.

What you'll see: bodies wrapped in white or red, carried on bamboo biers, cremated on stacked wood so the soul is freed and the ashes can go to the river. There's an electric crematorium in the building behind the steps doing the same sacrament faster.

Rules, non-negotiable: no photos of pyres, bodies or mourners. No staring. Keep to the upper steps, keep moving, and wave off donation hustlers with folded hands. Manikarnika, the great burning ghat, comes later — consider this the rehearsal.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open ghat, no ticket. Decline paid guiding offers firmly; donations to pandas or Doms are voluntary and never obligatory.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Cremations happen through the day and night.
stops.accessibility: Steep steps with no ramps. Stay on the upper terrace if the lower steps feel unsteady — the view and the lesson are the same.
stops.insiderTip: The tall chimneyed building is the electric crematorium — many local families use it, and its presence is a reminder that this is a working civic facility, not a spectacle.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north along the steps for just two to three minutes. The next stop is the colourful red-and-white striped temple rising directly over the river, almost next door.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Vrinda, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Kedar Ghat and Kedareshwar Temple
stops.narration:
Notice the accent change. Kedareshwar is Shiva — the destroyer-and-transformer god at the heart of all this — in the form India's south knows best, and this ghat belongs by tradition to southern and Bengali pilgrims who have been coming here for centuries. You will hear Tamil, Telugu and Bengali mixing with the Hindi on the steps, and the priests switch languages without breaking rhythm. Varanasi collects India's regions the way the river collects tributaries.

The temple itself is striped red and white and rises straight out of the steps. Behind it sits the kund, a square stepped temple tank that hosts festivals where the water turns into a mirror of lamps. Come back for one if you can: a kund festival is Diwali — the autumn festival of lights — compressed into a courtyard.

Practical note, since Manikarnika later is strictly no cameras: here, photograph freely, bathers at a distance, never close up. The ghats get grander and busier from here north, and this is the last stretch of riverfront that still feels like a neighbourhood.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open ghat and temple courtyard, no ticket. Small voluntary offerings at the shrine are customary but optional.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. The temple shrine is generally open from early morning to midday and again in the evening; hours shift seasonally.
stops.accessibility: Steep steps with no ramps. The temple platform above the steps is level once you climb up.
stops.insiderTip: Step into the lane just behind the temple for chai — the stalls here serve pilgrims, not tourists, so it is cheap, strong and fast.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue north along the ghats for about ten minutes, passing Narad, Raja and Munshi ghats. Follow the river bend — the next stop is the grand, wide ghat with the rows of umbrellas and the big evening stage, which you cannot miss.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: J Duval, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Dashashwamedh Ghat
stops.narration:
This is the main stage. Dashashwamedh — ten-horse-sacrifice — is named for the spot where Brahma, the creator god of the Hindu trinity, supposedly performed ten ashvamedha rites, the grandest ritual a king could stage: sacrifice a horse, claim the land it wandered. Ten of them, in one place, tells you this bend in the river was prime real estate even to the gods.

By day it is gloriously ordinary: marigold sellers, barbers shaving pilgrims' heads for mourning rites, boatmen shouting destinations. Then at sunset it turns into theatre. The Ganga aarti — a fire offering where priests on tiered platforms swing giant tiered lamps in synchronized circles to conch shells and chanting — runs about three quarters of an hour, starting around seven, season permitting. Get here an hour early for a step, or watch from a boat, which costs a few hundred rupees to hire between several of you.

What you're watching is devotion as public spectacle, and there is nothing cynical about saying so: the priests are performers and believers at once, and the crowd — pilgrims, tourists, pickpockets, all rapt — is half the show.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open ghat, no ticket for the aarti, whether you watch from the steps or the water. Shared boats for the evening aarti typically run about ₹200 to ₹500 per person; fix the price and duration before boarding.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. The evening Ganga aarti begins around 7pm most of the year, shifting slightly with the season — confirm the day's time locally. Morning aarti runs near sunrise.
stops.accessibility: Wide, relatively even steps by ghat standards, but still no ramps and no handrails. The crowds at aarti time are dense; arrive early for a stable spot on the upper steps.
stops.insiderTip: The steps beat the boats. Boats drift, jostle and charge surge prices — a high step near the centre gives you the full synchronised-lamp view for free.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the ghat by the main steps up to the street and walk inland, away from the river, for about eight minutes through the lanes. The next stop is the temple with the golden towers at the end of the new corridor — follow the signs for Shri Kashi Vishwanath Dham.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Sujay25, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Kashi Vishwanath Temple and Corridor
stops.narration:
Up the lane is one of the twelve jyotirlingas — self-manifested pillars of Shiva's light, the holiest category of Shiva shrine there is. This one, Kashi Vishwanath, is the most famous of the twelve, which is exactly why it has been destroyed and rebuilt more times than any temple should have to survive.

The short version, stated plainly. The Mughals — the Muslim emperors who ruled much of India from the 1500s to the 1700s — demolished it more than once across the centuries, including Aurangzeb's order in 1669. After that demolition the Gyanvapi mosque rose beside the ruins, and it still stands there, its status disputed in court to this day. The present gold-spired temple is mostly the work of Ahilyabai Holkar, queen of the Marathas — the Hindu warrior confederacy that rose as Mughal power faded — in 1780. Two faiths' holiest ground, one courtyard wall apart, lawyers included. Hold that fact gently and move on. The city has.

Then, in 2021, the Kashi Vishwanath Corridor bulldozed the surrounding maze to open a grand marble walkway from the river to the shrine. Quicker darshan — the auspicious viewing of the deity that pilgrims queue for — cleaner sightlines, demolished homes and temples along the way. Praised and mourned in roughly equal measure, like everything else here.

Practical: go at dawn, expect lines and airport-grade security, phones and cameras stay outside. The pandas — hereditary pilgrim priests who keep families' records and arrange rituals for a fee — will find you; decide in advance whether you want one. A paid Sugam Darshan ticket, a few hundred rupees, buys a shorter queue. Check the current figure. The god can wait. The line cannot be hurried.
stops.entranceFeeNote: General entry to the temple is free. A paid Sugam Darshan express queue, around ₹300, is usually available. Lockers for phones and bags are free or nominal. Rules, prices and ID requirements change often, so verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Generally open from about 3am to 11pm, with sanctum closures duringarti periods. Security lines are shortest in the early morning and longest on Mondays and festival days.
stops.accessibility: The new corridor is wide, paved and mostly level — the easiest walking on this tour. The temple sanctum itself involves crowds, queuing and steps, and is difficult for anyone with limited mobility.
stops.insiderTip: Do not carry your phone to the gate and hope for the best — leave it at your hotel or use the lockers first. The frisking queues move slowly and rejoining them costs you an hour.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk back out to the lanes west of the temple and turn into the narrow bazaar lane heading towards Godowlia. The next stop is the food strip a few minutes' walk away — follow the smell of frying ghee.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Gannu03, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Vishwanath Gali Food Lanes
stops.narration:
Turn downhill into Vishwanath Gali, where the pilgrims eat. Varanasi does breakfast with the seriousness other cities reserve for elections: kachori-sabzi — puffed bread, spiced potato curry — chased with syrup-crisp jalebi, those orange whirlpools of fried batter, served well into the afternoon by stalls that have not changed their menus in generations.

Winter brings the miracle: malaiyo, a foam sweet the vendors swear is churned from morning dew and saffron. Food science disagrees about the dew. Nobody argues with the taste — it vanishes from the stalls by mid-morning, so this is a now-or-next-year situation.

Then find the Blue Lassi shop, running for generations on curd, fruit and attitude, served thick in kulhads, the little clay cups you toss when done. And finish the education with paan: betel leaf, areca nut, lime paste, an engineering of mild stimulants the vendor folds to order. It stains, it buzzes faintly, and refusing it politely is a complete social skill here. Watch one being made even if you pass — the folding alone is worth it.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Street food is pay-as-you-go: kachori-sabzi around ₹30 to ₹60 a plate, lassi ₹40 to ₹120 depending on flavour. Prices vary by stall, so treat these as a guide.
stops.openingHours: Stalls serve from early morning to late evening. Breakfast items run out by late morning; lassi shops pour all day.
stops.accessibility: Narrow, crowded, uneven lanes with no seating in most stalls. Expect to stand or perch on steps; the ground can be greasy near fry stalls.
stops.insiderTip: Ask for the kulhad — the clay cup — for your lassi, and eat the malai topping with a spoon first. The malaiyyo, if it is winter, sells out by mid-morning, so go early.
stops.nextStopDirections: Head back east towards the river through the lanes, about five minutes downhill. The next stop is the riverside terrace above the cremation ghat — follow the signs for Manikarnika and stay on the upper path.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Adam Jones, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Manikarnika Ghat Viewpoint
stops.narration:
Drop your voice to half. Below is Manikarnika, the great burning ghat — Kashi's crematorium-in-chief, barely gone out in centuries. The story: Shiva's earring — mani, jewel; karna, ear — dropped here while he danced with his wife Parvati, consecrating the ground forever. The sacred fire below is said to have burned since, lit by Shiva himself and kept ever since by the Dom community, who have run these pyres for generations.

The arithmetic of the place: scores of cremations a day, every day. Wood smoke, chanting, marigold, grief handled at industrial scale and total sincerity at once. Nobody below considers this morbid. A cremation here is the single greatest gift the living can arrange for the dead.

So this is a viewpoint, not a visit. Stay on the upper path. Do not go down among the pyres. Do not photograph anything that burns or anyone who mourns — a camera here will rightly get you shouted at. Decline the rooftop-view hustlers with folded hands.

And while you stand here, notice what surrounds the dying: laundry lines, cricket, chai smoke, boatmen arguing. Varanasi refuses to segregate death from life, and after five minutes of watching, the arrangement starts to look less strange than everything else we do instead.
stops.entranceFeeNote: No ticket. Do not pay for rooftop or guided views of the burning platforms; observe briefly and freely from the public riverside path.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Cremations continue through the day and night; visit in daylight for the clearest, most respectful viewing from the path.
stops.accessibility: The viewpoint is on the upper riverside path with steps nearby and no ramps. Do not attempt the lower burning terraces, which are uneven, crowded and inappropriate for visitors to enter.
stops.insiderTip: Put the camera away entirely at this stop — not just the shutter, the visible camera. The kindest thing you can do here is be obviously, deliberately not photographing.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue north along the riverside path for about three minutes, past Lalita Ghat. The next stop is the ghat with the half-sunken temple leaning in the shallows, just ahead.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Gannu03, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Scindia Ghat
stops.narration:
At the waterline sits a Shiva temple doing its best impression of a sinking ship — tilted sideways, half underwater, sanctum flooded. The Maratha Scindias of Gwalior — a Maratha clan who ruled that central Indian city — built this ghat in the 1830s, temple included, and it started leaning almost immediately. Too heavy for the riverbank, the engineers say; the river shifted, say the priests; the gods objected to the architecture, say the regulars. Whatever the cause, nobody knocked it down — the sanctum floods every monsoon and worship carries on regardless.

This is the quiet end of the riverfront, and the tour ends here on purpose. The crowds thin, the touts give up, and the old palaces stand along the bank in evening light. Turn around: on a clear evening you can see the whole curve of the ghats back to Assi, lamps coming on one by one. You started at dawn with bells. You end at dusk with lamps. The river, unimpressed by both, keeps flowing.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open ghat, no ticket. The Nepali temple behind the ghat is free to view from outside.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Late afternoon and sunset give the best light on the sunken temple and the southward view.
stops.accessibility: Steep, uneven steps with no ramps. The sunken temple area itself is partly collapsed — admire it from the stable upper steps.
stops.insiderTip: Look south from the top steps at dusk: the full crescent of lighted ghats is the best panoramic photograph of the walk, and nobody crowds this end.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Climb to the lane behind the ghat and follow it south back towards Godowlia for rickshaws and taxis, or stroll the ghat-top path back towards Dashashwamedh for the evening aarti boats.
